summary: The 1906 octagonal wooden front tower of the 1894 North Channel range on Grosse Ile in the Detroit River; the rear tower is gone; township-owned, entry by appointment.

lens.where: removed by the Coast Guard at the 1963 extinguishing (Water Trails)

structures.type: octagonal wooden tower on concrete foundations
structures.note: Rebuilt 1906 on concrete foundations (LighthouseFriends); the 1894 front stood on wooden pilings.

staffing.note: Keepers until 1920 (LighthouseFriends). The Commissioner's report for fiscal 1921 calls the Fighting Island system nonattended, under observation of a keeper in the locality.

access.note: Township-owned; entry by appointment, arranged through the Grosse Ile Historical Society; can be viewed from the water (Water Trails). Not readily visible from land (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: Grosse Ile Township (owner); Grosse Ile Historical Society (maintains)

events.note: Act approved 5 August 1892 appropriated $2,500 for a second pair of range lights on Grosse Isle.
Two beacons completed in June and first exhibited on July 16, 1894.
Keeper's dwelling built beside the rear light; Congress provided $3,500 in February 1903.
Front tower rebuilt on concrete foundations; the octagonal wooden tower of today.
Water Trails dates the end of the North Channel and its rear light to the opening of the Livingstone Channel in 1912.
LighthouseFriends: the North Channel rear range light was discontinued in 1917 and the front light retained and renamed Grosse Isle Lighthouse.
LighthouseFriends: the light was automated in 1920 and keeper James T. Story transferred to Windmill Point.

Commissioner's report: works on the Fighting Island channel completed June 1921; an acetylene light in a fifth-order lens installed in the old frame tower at Grosse Isle (the range is not named, so it is not confirmed that this is the front tower); system nonattended.
Light extinguished; the Fresnel lens removed by the Coast Guard (Water Trails; LighthouseFriends gives 1963 for the decommissioning).
Township bought the tower from the Department of the Interior for $350, with funds from the Grosse Ile Historical Society.
Restoration started: a steel sheet-piling foundation placed around the corroded foundation.
Listed in the Coast Guard's 2013 Light List as a private aid to navigation, one second on and one second off (LighthouseFriends).

keepers.note: In charge of the North Channel range from 1911; kept the Grosse Isle light until automation in 1920; transferred to Windmill Point (LighthouseFriends).

other_stations.name: Windmill Point Light
other_stations.note: LighthouseFriends: transferred there when the Grosse Isle light was automated in 1920 (start year from LighthouseFriends). The Commissioner's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1922 names James T. Story as assistant keeper at Windmill Point Light Station (cite 11). The end of the service is not given.

notes_for_editor: (1) Keepers: Watson and Kean come from LighthouseFriends only. Story's dates (1911-1920) come from LighthouseFriends; the Commissioner's fiscal 1922 report names him as assistant keeper at Windmill Point (note 11). The Light-House Board reports read here do not name keepers, and the Official Register (not in the corpus) was not checked. The newspaper search for 'Grosse Isle' with 'range' and 'light' (Michigan papers, 1894-1921) returned 28 pages, mostly unrelated Detroit Times items; none was read for this station. (2) Disputed dates: rear range discontinued 1917 (LighthouseFriends) vs after the 1912 Livingstone Channel opening (Water Trails); automation 1920 (LighthouseFriends, Story's transfer) vs the Commissioner's June 1921 completion of the Fighting Island works. The Commissioner's passage says 'at Grosse Isle' without naming which range; whether the 'old frame tower' is this front tower is not stated, and the story does not claim it is; it says the report does not name the range. (3) Status: the record says inactive. Water Trails says the light was 'permanently extinguished in 1963', but LighthouseFriends says the 2013 Light List carried it as a private aid with a one-second flash. This needs the current Light List before the status changes. (4) The South Channel range (us-mi-grosse-isle-south-channel-range-front) and its records are not part of this story. The 3 September 1894 blow-down cited in the Storms chapter belongs to the South Channel range and is labelled as such. (5) us-mi-grosse-isle-north-channel-range-rear is hidden and merged into this record; the rear-range facts are in this file. (6) Scan pages are cited because printed page numbers could not be confirmed. The 1891 text reads 'Ballards Keef' and 'Fighting Istand' in OCR; the story uses the printed spelling 'Ballards Reef' and 'Fighting Island'. (7) Access: the record's 'public' conflicts with Water Trails' 'by appointment only' (see corrections). (8) Water Trails and LighthouseFriends are copyrighted sites: the story paraphrases them with short quotations. (9) No general-period context passages were used. (10) Fact-check 2026-10-28: the 1892 report (scan 532) says the private lights were not put in operation until a few nights after navigation opened in spring 1891, and that the City of Detroit accident 'would not have happened if Ballards Keef had then been lighted'. It does not say the private lights were at Ballards Reef; LighthouseFriends says a private light had been serving mariners on Ballard's Reef 'for some time' before the 1887 request for range lights. The story now uses the report's wording. (11) Story's Windmill Point post: the Commissioner's fiscal 1922 report (scan 756, the Eleventh District rescue list) names James T. Story as assistant keeper at Windmill Point Light Station; it is cited in the story and in other_stations. (12) USLHS roster for the matched place (the rear range record) lists no keepers ('ROSTER: none listed'), so the keeper names stand on LighthouseFriends and the Commissioner's 1922 report only.
